Never, on any timescale that matters. The premise is a myth. Room-temperature glass behaves as a solid, not a slow liquid.

Its viscosity at room temperature is estimated at 10²⁰ Pa·s or higher. Edgar Zanotto's 1998 calculation put the time for cathedral glass to flow visibly beyond the age of the universe. Later estimates using different glass compositions came out shorter but still around a billion years or more. Your windows will be replaced or broken long before they move a measurable amount.

The uneven thickness in old church windows comes from how the glass was made. Medieval crown and cylinder methods produced panes that varied in thickness, and glaziers often set the heavier edge at the bottom for stability. They didn't always do this, though, and some old panes are thicker at the top or sides, which flow can't explain. Other evidence points the same way: Roman glassware and centuries-old telescope lenses show no sagging, and those lenses would have lost their precise shapes if glass flowed.
